newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Sports shoemaker Yue Yuen puts best foot forward.
newsitem.headline: Sports shoemaker Yue Yuen puts best foot forward.

text.p: Behind such world famous names as Nike, Reebok and Adidas is a little known one, that of Yue Yuen Industrial Holdings Ltd.
Now the Hong Kong-based sports shoe maker is seeking to raise its profile among local and international investors.
"We would like to have more U.S. institutions interested in our stock," said Yue Yuen executive director Edward Ku.
"We feel Yue Yuen is probably the largest listed industrial company on the Hong Kong market and deserves to be looked upon more seriously by institutions," he told Reuters.

The company, one of the world's largest manufacturer of sports shoes and supplier to such famous brands as Nike Inc, Reebok International, and Adidas AG, recently consolidated its shares to make them easier to trade.
Shareholders approved a five-for-one share consolidation on March 27 and the new shares began trading on April 1.

The consolidation helped the shares rise to HK$18.90 on April 3, against their pre-consolidation close on March 27 at HK$3.20 each or HK$16.00 for five shares. The shares later eased back to close at HK$17.60 on April 15.
Analysts say the share consolidation was likely to be the first move in a strategy to seek a NASDAQ listing in the United States, but the company denies this.
"Right now, we do not have such a plan. Of course the board has considered all the alternatives," Ku said.
The point of the consolidation was to increase the share's attractiveness to U.S. institutions, not to reach a minimum NASDAQ price level, Ku said.
"Basically, we would not like it (our share) to be a penny stock in the (United) States," he added.
But the campaign to burnish the company's image was dealt a blow when a supervisor at one of the group's factories in Vietnam was accused of abusing workers.

A Taiwanese supervisor at Pou Chen Vietnam Enterprises Ltd, which makes shoes under contract to Nike, will stand trial for allegedly forcing 56 workers to jog twice around the two-km factory perimeter for failing to wear regulation workshoes.

Pou Chen Vietnam became a subsidiary of Yue Yuen when in September last year it bought the 55 percent of Taiwan-based Pou Yuen Industrial (Holdings) Ltd that it did not already own from Pou Chen Corp. The latter also holds 9.8 percent of Yue Yuen.
"We took immediate action to rectify ... The supervisor (responsible) has been discharged," said Ku. "The company has a strict code of conduct; no worker should be punished."

Nike spokeswoman Martha Benson said the U.S. shoemaker was not happy about the incident but added she did not believe the problem was systemic. Pou Chen Vietnam also launched a series of supervisor training programmes after the incident, she said.
"They really took the initiative to roll that programme out right away," she said.

Benson also said the Vietnam plant had been in operation for only about 18 months, whereas the group's older plants in Indonesia were notable for improved dormitories, added benefits, 24-hour medical care and other programmes.
Yue Yuen has six production lines in Vietnam, 24 in Indonesia and 115 in China.

Despite the bad publicity, analysts still like the stock, noting that Vietnam was only a very small part of the company. They added it was a candidate to join the Hong Kong stock market's blue-chip Hang Seng index in the future.
"It is possible that Yue Yuen could replace one of the constituent stocks ... that are little traded," said Vijay Harjani, investment analyst at BZW Securities Asia. (US$1 = HK$ 7.75)
